text: Two approaches are used, both longer and more involved than the standard Sitkum route. (1) Via the White Chuck River, no longer usable since a 2003 flood destroyed the trail and road: the old line followed the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about 6 miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail 1.7 miles up to the PCT. Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing (water) to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT on Glacier Ridge about 0.7 miles beyond the creek, which climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder. (2) Via North Fork Sauk Trailhead: North Fork Sauk Trail to White Pass (~9 miles, ~5,900 ft), then a long traverse north on/near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area — a 20-mile-plus approach day used by some parties. From high camp, the route proper begins by traversing the upper southwest slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to an 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers. Ascend the Kennedy Glacier — a 'crumbling mess' of loose moraine and boulders low down — to an 8,800 ft saddle where Frostbite Ridge proper begins. The ridge itself mixes loose pumice/dust scrambling on narrow, exposed steps with sections of steep snow (45–50°) protected with pickets or ice screws, passing directly beneath/through the Rabbit Ears — twin eroded lava pinnacles — where loose rock is a real hazard, especially in warm, dry conditions (cold, snowy conditions lock the rock in place and make the scramble more manageable). Above the Rabbit Ears the route steepens further into a section of alpine ice, anywhere from a single ~40-foot ice step to roughly 200 feet of AI2, typically simul-climbed with ice screw protection, before crossing the crater rim and descending briefly into the crater to reach the 10,550 ft summit.

edits.new: traversing across the Ptarmigan Glacier's upper southwest slopes, staying just under the ridgeline, to about 8,000 ft

text: Frostbite Ridge is essentially a one-way, committing line — once on the ridge there is no turning back — and virtually all parties descend a different, easier route rather than reversing the ridge. The standard descent is down the Sitkum Glacier: from the summit, descend the gully east of the summit into the upper Sitkum Glacier, traverse and descend to a saddle at roughly 8,000 ft, then continue down the lower Sitkum Glacier to Boulder Basin, picking up the climbers' path back to the PCT, then south on the PCT to White Pass and down the North Fork Sauk Trail to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead (some parties instead reverse to the Cool Glacier/Gerdine Ridge side if that's where their car is staged). The single rappel belongs to the ridge itself rather than to this walk-off descent: there is a natural belay-horn anchor (a rock horn, typically backed by old slings — inspect before trusting) just above the steep ice north of the Rabbit Ears, used to lower one pitch of steep ice into a notch referred to as the 'doorway gap' in the summit rib. This is a single-pitch rappel — a 30m single-strand rope is sufficient for the drop described — encountered while working through the crux ice/rock step near the Rabbit Ears (i.e., on the way up for most parties, since the standard descent avoids the ridge entirely); some parties simul-climb this step with screw/picket protection instead of rappelling, depending on ice conditions. Carry 3–4 ice screws and/or pickets for this section and for the steep snow/ice above the Rabbit Ears regardless of whether you end up rappelling it.

text: The twin eroded lava towers of the Rabbit Ears sit at the very top of the initial ridge and only look like ears once above them. Pass through the notch and downclimb about 150 ft of class 3 rock to a small saddle. The rock is very loose in warm, dry weather; cold, snowy conditions freeze it in place and make this section far more manageable.

text: From the saddle, cross snow or loose rock along the ridge to the foot of an alpine ice face and climb it for one to two pitches until it rounds off. Mostly around 50°, with a short step that has run 60° to near-vertical in some years; reported grades range AI1 to AI2. Bring screws and pickets, and a second tool eases the steep step.

text: Top out onto the crater rim, watching for cornices and hidden holes along its edge. Drop into the crater and climb its steep wall on the left, which may be hard ice low down with crevasses opening late in the season, then make an easy traverse to a gap on the right and a short climb to the summit.

text:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. That saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are not visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

text: From Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft), traverse SE onto the Sitkum Glacier and ascend a corridor on its left (climber's) side heading NE toward a saddle near 9,500 ft by Sitkum Spire. From the saddle, follow the pumice ridge toward the summit, staying right of and below the peak, then finish up a snow chute to the top. Crevasse danger is generally minimal and the route rarely steepens significantly.

text: Climb slightly south to the corridor beside the rock feature that splits the lower glacier, then trend northeast. Above that gap the angle eases. Aim for the saddle near 9,500 ft just east of Sitkum Spire, the obvious rock finger on the west summit ridge. Crevasses are not abundant but include hidden ones, even low down, and late season turns stretches to bare ice. Leave camp early, before the snow softens.

text:
From the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass at about 4,400 ft, head south on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly nine to ten miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp, then up the increasingly brushy North Fork trail.

About two miles up it, leave the trail at an obvious clearing before Grizzly Creek and bushwhack steeply through slide alder and timber to the toe of the arete. Carrying on past Grizzly Creek to the ford and the slabs beside the waterfall leads to the Goode Glacier and the Northeast Buttress, not to this ridge.

The total approach is on the order of twelve or more miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing. Most parties bivy low on the ridge; water is reliable along Bridge Creek and scarce once you are on the rock, so tank up before you leave the creek.

The first ascent climbed its first fifth-class pitch at dusk and bivied on a bench, with the real difficulty starting the next morning.

text: Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway (19.3 miles east of the Verlot Public Service Center), on the Weeden Creek Trail / Gothic Basin trail (USFS #724). The first ~0.7 mile follows an old closed mining road before singletrack begins climbing steadily through forest; the trail fords Weeden Creek around the 1.1-mile mark (no bridge — the main reliable water source low on the route). From there the trail switchbacks up a steep, root-and-rock staircase, gaining close to 1,000 ft/mile through a roughly 2-mile crux band; this section holds lingering snow patches and old avalanche run-out debris across the tread well into early summer in heavy-snow years, and can require an ice axe. Around 3.5–4 miles the trail breaks out of timber into the open slabs and tarns of Gothic Basin (around 5,000 ft) — the last dependable water before the final push and a good bail-out point in poor weather. From the basin, continue up talus and slab benches roughly another 0.5–0.6 mile to the saddle above Foggy Lake (total to the lake is about 9.2 miles / 2,800–3,100 ft round trip per multiple trail sources), then drop slightly and traverse roughly 0.3–0.4 mile along/above the lake's shore to its outlet. At the outlet, leave the maintained tread for an intermittent, cairned climber's path onto Gothic Peak's SE ridge; stay in the scree climber's-right of the ridge crest rather than on the crest itself, following cairns past a small tarn at the base of a snowfield and up broken rock to the base of the summit block. Route-finding is the main approach-specific hazard: in early season, snow can bury the cairned line, and many parties inadvertently stray onto exposed Class 4 rock to climber's-left of the correct, easier line just below the summit block.

edits.old: stay in the scree climber's-right of the ridge crest rather than on the crest itself
edits.new: keep to the scree on the climber's right of the ridge crest instead of on the crest itself

text: The scramble begins at the lake's outlet, not from a random point on the shore, and getting on it early or late is the usual error. From the outlet, look up at the obvious low point on Gothic's southeast ridge. The line is not the ridge crest: stay in the scree on the climber's right of the crest and follow the cairns, which are numerous and continuous, past a small tarn at the foot of a snowfield. Cairns underfoot and scree, not rock, is the confirmation. At the very top, where the summit block stops the scree, cut left onto a narrow sidewalk of downsloping rock — slightly exposed easy friction — and switchback back up and right to the base of the block; the final scramble is about 30 ft of low-exposure class 3. Two negatives: if you are on the crest itself you have drifted left off the easy line, and if you find yourself on exposed class 4 to climber's left just below the summit block you have gone too far left, which is where most parties who get into trouble end up. In early season the cairns can be buried and the correct line is genuinely hard to hold.

text:
The climb begins where the tread ends, and the arrival test is the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy. You know you are there because the trail stops going up in a line and the ground opens on both sides — navigation shifts from following tread to reading a ridge. There is also a signed Olympic National Park boundary marker in a saddle on this stretch and a spring path dropping off the crest. From here on you are on the crest and the crest is the route.

The test that actually matters on this route is at the far end, and it is a false summit with a name and a number: point 7076. From below, 7076 reads as the summit. It is not. The true summit of Gray Wolf is 7,218 ft and it lies further north along the crest and is higher. So the fog rule is simple: after Baldy you drop about 600 ft, climb back up over a prominent bump, and that bump is not the top. Keep going north over the last of the talus, detouring briefly round the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short Class 2-3 scramble on loose rock. If you turned round on the first big bump past Baldy, you turned round on 7076.

Second test, on the way to 7076 itself: the crest gets steeper and broken approaching it. The published avoidance is to traverse west at about 6,500 ft and then swing back to gain 7076 by its northwest aspect, and to stay in the basin below and right of the broken rock ridge until you can gain the saddle between the twin summits — 7076 has twin tops with snowfields between them. There is no trail at these decision points, which is why they are written down.

Third test, earlier: Point 6537 is a rocky gendarme and false summit below Baldy, normally skirted on its south side rather than climbed over. If you are scrambling straight over a tower before you have reached Baldy, you have taken the crest too literally.

Honest limit: long stretches of this crest are unmarked and off-trail and the whole thing is above treeline. Carry a map or GPS; the ridge is the handrail but the summit identification is not obvious by eye.

edits.new: to keep to the basin beneath and to the right of the broken rock ridge until the saddle between the twin summits can be gained

text: Gunsight Peak is a multi-towered granite spire in the remote Dome Peak massif of the Glacier Peak Wilderness, guarded by the Chikamin Glacier to the west and Blue Glacier to the east. It neighbors Dome and Sinister Peaks on the classic Ptarmigan Traverse and requires a full 2-day approach (either from Downey Creek in the west or Stehekin/Agnes Creek in the east) before any climbing begins. The true summit is a tiny horn of rock roughly the size of a barstool, and parties typically take turns tagging it.

text: A reddish-black basalt dike is the line, and it is softer than everything around it. From the 7,000 ft snow dome and rock outcrop, boot up the snow finger between the main and south spires; from a breach in that finger, a short wall leads to a broad ledge, then leftward to a steep dihedral of black rock whose top fifteen feet is the exposed 5.6 crux on solid granite. Above it, traverse left on Class 3 granite into a distinctive dike of reddish-black basalt — this is the feature that carved the gunsight notch in the first place, eroding faster than the granite either side, so if the rock you are on is the same colour as its neighbours you are not in the dike. It scrambles easily, if loosely, to the high notch between the main and north spires. There a vertical headwall blocks a direct exit: descend about twenty feet and traverse right across steep, solid, well-broken rock into a shallow parallel gully. Short chimneys and cracks to 5.5 end at the crest beside a large horn slung with old rappel tat — that horn is not the summit; the summit is a separate horn about the size of a barstool further along the ridge.

text:
Same problem and same ground as the rest of the west face. The roads named 'Strasse' off the Alpental access road are private; since 2021 the Alpental Community Club has forbidden both driving and walking on them, and climbers have been confronted by residents. The talus field has to be reached by a line that avoids private land, and no established path exists.

The route begins at the top of the talus cone below the face. Reckon on roughly half an hour to an hour from wherever you park to the top of the cone, and wear a helmet on the talus.

Climbing continues via mixed scrambling and rock sections to the summit. Route involves significant high-consequence scrambling.

Descend north past the middle and north summits toward the Cave Ridge saddle and back to the trailhead.

text: Park at Alpental near the Snow Lake Trailhead and start up the unsigned Cave Ridge/Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail beginning about 100 ft south of the Snow Lake Trail. From a large clearing around 4000-4200 ft, climb to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, then turn right (south) and follow the ridge to Guye's north summit — class 3 in summer. The 'Hidden Ridge' variation continues from the north summit around an outcropping to a hidden ridge with one 5.4 move (otherwise class 4), rappelling ~30 ft off a slung horn to the notch between the north and middle summits; this was found to be a more direct, more enjoyable line than the standard gully descent in winter/spring conditions.

edits.new: rappelling ~30 ft off a slung horn into the notch separating the north and middle summits

text: The documented north-side line to Guye Peak leaves from the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,080-3,120 ft) via the separate, unsigned Cave Ridge/Snoqualmie Mountain boot path, which splits off about 100 ft south of the Snow Lake Trail sign — this is a different trailhead path than the West Face/Improbable Traverse talus approach. Follow it up to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak (roughly 1.5 miles, reported around 4,500-4,600 ft). From the saddle, turn right (south) and follow the ridge toward Guye's north summit; the standard line follows a steep gully system rated class 3 in summer. Climber-triggered rockfall is common on the talus and gully sections, so a helmet is worth wearing once off-trail. A short 'Hidden Ridge' variation near the north summit traverses right to an outcropping where a horn can be slung for a single ~30 ft rappel into the north/middle notch, adding one 5.4 move of class 4/low-5th climbing.

text:
From the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead area (about 3,080-3,120 ft), take the unmarked climbers' boot path that leaves the pavement close to the Snow Lake trail sign — the one that serves Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, not the west-face talus approach. Follow it up to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, roughly a mile and a half in and reported around 4,500-4,600 ft.

From the saddle, turn right (south) and work toward Guye's north summit. Helmets are worth wearing from the point you leave the trail; climber-triggered rockfall is common on the talus and in the gully.

This peak is also reached from the northbound PCT trailhead through Commonwealth Basin, which is the east side of the mountain — a different approach to a different aspect.

text: Do not plan on downclimbing the gully; at 70 degrees near the top with minimal protection it is a bad retreat. From the ridge between the true and false summits, the standard exit is over the top and out on foot. Going west, drop from the Guye / Cave Ridge saddle onto the climbers' trail down to the Alpental parking area, which then leaves a road walk of roughly a mile back to a car parked on the Commonwealth side. Going east, reverse the Commonwealth Basin approach back to the PCT North trailhead, which is the natural choice if that is where you left the car. In winter both descents cross avalanche terrain of their own, and the west-side bootpath is easily lost under snow - carry a track or a bearing.

text: A short winter day. From the PCT North trailhead, hike about 1.4 miles up the old Commonwealth Basin trail until the peak is directly west-northwest, then break uphill to the base of the gully. Climb 1,400 ft of snow that steepens from 45 to about 70 degrees, top out on the ridge between the true and false summits, and walk off east down Commonwealth or west over Cave Ridge. Start before dawn so the gully is still frozen: the sun-exposed half of the route softens quickly and the entire line becomes a wet-slide problem once it warms. There is nothing here that justifies an overnight.

text:
Take a bearing, because this one can be done blind. Walk the old Commonwealth Basin trail about 1.4 miles until the summit of Guye bears roughly 290 degrees — west-northwest — from you, then turn and go straight uphill. The start of the route is at about 47.4411, -121.4026. In cloud that pair of numbers settles it and nothing on the ground has to be seen.

What the ground should do, in order, once you commit: the route starts by going 45 degrees straight up. Only then does the gully proper develop, turning northwest for about 40 m and steepening as it turns. After that it runs directly at the summit, which stays visible for much of the climb on a clear day. If the ground you are on stays uniformly angled and never turns northwest, you are on the open slope beside the gully rather than in it.

The angle is the other test: this is the steepest of Guye's gully lines. About 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then progressively steeper, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. A gully that stays moderate all the way is one of the peak's other lines.

Where it puts you: it finishes at the ridge between the true and false summits — not on a summit. If your line tops out on a summit block, it is not this one.

And a conditions test that is part of the finding here: roughly half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which is what gives it solid snow under the surface. It also means the two halves can be in quite different condition on a warm day.

edits.old: it finishes at the ridge between the true and false summits
edits.new: it finishes at the ridge that links the true and false summits

text: From Glacier, WA, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 1 mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS 39); turn right, then take an immediate left onto Deadhorse Road (FS 37). FS 37 normally continues 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide Trailhead. FS 37 has been closed by the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1, and during the repair work it is gated near its start (mile 0.03), so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle; check the road's status before planning around it. When open, hike Skyline Divide Trail #678 through old-growth forest switchbacks and into meadows on the ridge crest (~2 mi), follow the crest to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft, ~4.5 mi), then continue cross-country along the open ridge to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley Peak.

text: Drop off the saddle through open heather and easy slopes into the Diobsud basin, aiming for the uppermost pair of the four Diobsud Lakes. Heather and open ground with route-finding required, but no technical terrain. On-file timing puts this camp at roughly 6 to 6.5 hours and about 7.4 miles from the trailhead, with around 3,600 ft of gain and 500 ft of loss, and it is the standard base for the south-slopes climb.

text: From the col at the southwest end of the crags, make a rising, crevasse- and moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier to reach the second col, the one between Hagan's twin summits. This short glacier section is the technical crux of the route despite the Class 2-3 billing: carry rope, harness and a crevasse-rescue kit, and put crampons on - both are recommended even in midsummer. The moat is the same hazard in both directions on the way back. From the twin-summit col a short Class 2-3 scramble on slabs gains the summit ridge. Hagan carries several rocky bumps of similar height along that crest, so identify the true high point (7,067-7,080 ft) before committing to the last moves.

edits.old: make a rising, crevasse- and moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier to reach
edits.new: make a rising traverse, watching for crevasses and the moat, around the Hagan Glacier's ice apron to reach

text: Park at the Baker River Trailhead, the end of FR 11 (Baker Lake Highway), elevation roughly 800 ft. Start on Baker River Trail #606, which follows the true-right bank of the Baker River upstream through mossy old-growth forest — mostly flat, easy tread. At about 0.6 mile the trail crosses the river on a suspension bridge. Shortly after, a rerouted section drops steeply down a bank to ford a side creek and climbs back out through deadfall; this crossing gets wet and can be genuinely difficult or impassable during high runoff (spring snowmelt or after heavy rain) — plan around low-water conditions. The trail then enters North Cascades National Park and continues roughly another mile to Sulphide Creek Camp near the Sulphide Creek/Baker River confluence, about 2.6 miles and only ~170 ft of gain from the trailhead — this is the last maintained tread, the last reliable easy water, and a common bivy for a two-day trip. From near Sulphide Creek Camp, leave the trail and begin a steep, unmarked, use-path-at-best bushwhack climbing north/northeast up the valley wall through old growth and brush toward a small unnamed tarn at roughly 4550-4600 ft informally called 'Hidden Lake' (not the maintained, signed Hidden Lake Trail #745 near Marblemount, which is a different area entirely) — this gains close to 3,700 ft in a little over a mile with no tread. From the tarn, continue bushwhacking north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands that form the route-finding crux of the approach; parties pick brushy ramps and weaknesses to keep the grade climbable. Above the cliffbands the forest breaks into open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank around 6000-6400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. From the benches, ascend a broad talus-and-scree couloir to the southwest end of the Hagan Mountain crags, then make a rising, crevasse/moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier (rope and crampons recommended even in summer) to reach the col between Hagan's twin summits, finishing with a short Class 2-3 scramble on slabs to the summit (listed 7067-7080 ft). Overall this is one of the more sustained, taxing approaches in the North Cascades — heavy old-growth/slide-alder bushwhacking, two cliffband route-finding sections, loose scree, and a glacier crossing — which is why it is very commonly combined with Mount Blum (and sometimes Bacon Peak) into a multi-day traverse rather than done as a single out-and-back day.

edits.new: a rising traverse, mindful of crevasses and the moat, around the Hagan Glacier's ice apron

text: The pass sits between the south and middle peaks, and it is the south peak you climb. Arriving at 6,831 ft, you should have a summit on either hand: this is a pass between two of Hagan's own peaks, not a col on the outside of the massif, and if only one side of you rises to rock you are in the wrong gap. The climbing then goes up the south peak's north side to a notch on its upper east side — that notch is high on the peak, not at the pass, and it is on the east flank, so a notch you can walk into from the west is the wrong one. From the notch, traverse onto the south face and gain the summit ridge, work up a spur on the east, then bear around to the south, where slabs lead to the summit at Class 3. The finish is south-facing slab, not a gully: if you are grovelling up a loose gully at the top you have missed the traverse around to the south side.

text: Start in the deep notch north of the peak and climb the broad buttress above it toward the ridge crest. The first pitch has hollow, friable rock that improves steadily on the second. From there the line stays on the crest or just west of it, belaying at ledges, with steeper crack climbing in the middle of the route. High on the ridge a pitch traverses the west side of the narrowing crest with big exposure over the west face before working back to the crest. The last pitch is easy climbing on the crest, then a short scramble to the summit. Seven pitches is the usual count; belay at the obvious ledges rather than running pitches together, which causes rope drag.

edits.new: Begin in the deep notch lying north of the peak, then climb the broad buttress above it

text: Helmet Butte is normally climbed as part of a Buck Creek Pass backpacking trip rather than a car-to-car day climb, given the ~17.6-mile round-trip approach. From a point at 5,600 ft on the Buck Creek Pass Trail ('Waypoint 86'), the recommended line turns off-trail toward Pass No Pass on a well-defined but braiding boot path, gains a notch around 7,200 ft below the summit block, then finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 3 scramble on solid rock, aiming for the block's south (left) side for the easiest line. An alternate line continues past the trail junction to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble - this option is likely hazardous when wet.

edits.new: then climbs steep slopes of grass and heather up to the west side of the summit block

text: Follow Rachel Lake Trail #1313 about 2 miles to a brushy avalanche clearing near 3,300 ft; just past it take the unmarked climbers' path uphill on the right. Pass the first cliff band on the right, go left around an outcrop, and take a gully on the right through the second band. Climb the meadow and talus to the south side of the summit block, traverse east to the east-side gully, and climb its short class 3 notch to the top.

edits.new: Climb the meadow and talus up to the summit block's south side

text: Start at the Rachel Lake Trailhead (Trail #1313, elev. ~2,800 ft) at the end of Box Canyon Road/FR-4930. Follow the Rachel Lake Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the Box Canyon Creek drainage — the grade is easy and well-graded here, mostly Class 1 hiking. At roughly 2–2.2 miles and about 450–500 ft of gain (~3,300 ft elevation), the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing where Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast; this clearing is the key landmark. Just past it (some parties note it's after the second such clearing), watch on the right/climber's-right side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path (the 'Hibox climbers' path') leaving the maintained trail and heading northeast/uphill into the forest — it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. From here the character changes completely: the bootpath climbs steeply (mostly Class 2, with fallen timber to step over) before breaking out of the trees near a band of cliffs around 5,300 ft. Stay right of this first rock band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continuing through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band; a gully on the right provides passage through it. Above this the trail opens into a large sloping subalpine meadow (wildflowers in season) that funnels into a loose talus/scree slope — this is the most tedious and slip-prone section of the route, so careful foot placement matters more than pace. A thready boot path threads up through the talus to the south side of the summit block. There is no reliable water past the lower forest/creek section, so carry what you need from the car or treat water low on the mountain. The route-finding through the two cliff bands and the avalanche-path junction low on the trail are the two spots parties most often go astray; a GPS track or recent trip report beta is worth having.

edits.old: A thready boot path threads up through the talus to the south side of the summit block.
edits.new: A thready boot path threads up through the talus toward the summit block's south side.

text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than glissading the scree, which is loose and eroded. From the summit, downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block (good rock, low exposure, easy Class 3 moves), then pick your way back down through the loose talus/scree field to the sloping meadow. Some parties descend via a slightly different line on the east side of the summit block/east ridge before rejoining the ascent boot path lower down — functionally the same route, just avoid cutting new paths through the scree to limit erosion. Continue down through the two cliff bands (reversing right/left as on the way up) and back into the timber, staying alert for the boot path's exit point onto the maintained Rachel Lake Trail near the ~3,300 ft avalanche clearing — it's easy to miss in the trees when descending. Once back on Rachel Lake Trail #1313, it's an easy, well-graded 2+ miles back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required — the summit block's only technical move is a short, low-exposure Class 3 downclimb, not a rappel. Watch the weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in this range and parties often report hurrying off the loose upper slopes ahead of incoming storms.

edits.old: downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block
edits.new: downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the summit block's south side
